passages.text: Draft Genome Sequences of 14 <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</italic> Phages Isolated from Cattle Slurry

The diversity of bacteriophages in slurry from dairy cows remains largely unknown. <sentence_start/>Here, we report the draft genome sequences of 14 bacteriophages isolated from dairy cow slurry using <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</italic> K-12 MG1655 as a host.

There are approximately 1.8 million head of dairy cattle in the United Kingdom, producing a total of ~14 billion liters of milk per annum. <sentence_start/>Millions of tonnes of manure are produced by the UK dairy herd. <sentence_start/>The solid manure and liquid cow slurry produced by these animals is widely used as fertilizer and has the potential to allow the transmission of bacteria into the environment. <sentence_start/>There is concern that cattle slurry will allow the transmission of pathogenic bacteria and antibiotic resistance genes into soils (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chemosphere.2006.03.026" pmid="16677683" count="1">1</citation>), which ultimately may enter the human food chain. <sentence_start/>While the bacterial fraction of cattle slurry has been studied (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.mimet.2010.12.008" pmid="21167876" count="1">2</citation>), the viral fraction has not. <sentence_start/>Here, we examined the diversity of bacteriophages capable of infecting <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</italic>. <sentence_start/>A single slurry sample from a dairy farm slurry tank in the East Midlands of the United Kingdom was collected. <sentence_start/>The titer of phage capable of infecting <italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</italic> MG1655, was 4.43 × 10<sup>2</sup> (±1.2 × 10<sup>2</sup>) PFU/ml. <sentence_start/>A total of 30 bacteriophages were isolated, and 14 independent bacteriophage isolates were chosen at random for genome sequencing. <sentence_start/>Bacteriophage isolates were purified by a double overlay plaque assay (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-1-60327-164-6_7" pmid="19066811" count="1">3</citation>). <sentence_start/>DNA was extracted from 1 mL of crude lysates using a modified phenol:chloroform extraction method (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0168-6496(03)00247-2" pmid="19719564" count="1">4</citation>). <sentence_start/>One nanogram of input DNA was used to prepare a genomic library for sequencing, using the Illumina Nextera XT DNA sample kit per the manufacturer’s protocol (Illumina, USA). <sentence_start/>Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq instrument using the paired-end 2 × 250-bp protocol (version 2). <sentence_start/>Reads were trimmed with Sickle (<citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" count="1">5</citation>); genomes were assembled using SPAdes 3-1 with the “only-assembler” option (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1089/cmb.2012.0021" pmid="22506599" pmcid="PMC3342519" count="1">6</citation>). <sentence_start/>The sequence was further checked for errors by mapping reads against the resulting assembly with BWA-MEM using default settings, to correct any miscalled bases (<citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>).

The remapping of sequences allowed the complete circularly permuted genomes to be identified (slur02, slur03, slur04, slur07, slur08, slur11, slur13, and slur14). <sentence_start/>The exact termini of the remaining phages have not been experimentally determined. <sentence_start/>Assembled genomes were annotated with Prokka version 1.11 (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btu153" pmid="24642063" count="1">8</citation>) using a custom database constructed from all viral genomes available from EBI at the time. <sentence_start/>Bacteriophage genomes ranged in size from 43.9 kb (slur05) to 167.467 kb (slur08), and the G+C content ranged from 35.4% (slur14) to 54.5% (slur05). <sentence_start/>The most common type of bacteriophage isolated belonged to the genus <italic toggle="yes">T4likevirus</italic>, with eight bacteriophage isolates (slur02, slur03, slur04, slur07, slur08, slur11, slur13, and slur14) within this genus. <sentence_start/>In comparison to the archetypal phage T4, these isolates contained far fewer endonuclease-encoding genes (e.g., <italic toggle="yes">segD</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">segC</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">mobA</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">mobB</italic>). <sentence_start/>Homologues of the <italic toggle="yes">b-gt</italic> gene that encodes for β-glucosyltransferase, which glucosylates phage DNA and provides protection from host restriction enzymes, were also absent. <sentence_start/>Two HK578-like viruses (slur05 and slur06), along with two phages closely related to bacteriophage rv5 (slur16 and slur12), a T5-like phage (slur09) and a single phage (slur01) that had a high similarity to the previously novel enterotoxigenic <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> phage Seurat (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/genomeA.00044-15" pmid="25720682" pmcid="PMC4342423" count="1">9</citation>), were also isolated. <sentence_start/>This collection of phages expands our knowledge of phages associated with cattle slurry.

This whole-genome shotgun project has been deposited at DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank under the accession numbers (slur01), (slur02), (slur03), (slur04), (slur05), (slur06), (slur07), (slur08), (slur09), (slur11), (slur12)<bold>,</bold> (slur 13), (slur14), and (slur16).
